terms.gloss: go the wrong way; get it wrong
terms.grammar: used absolutely, or viā errāre, take the wrong road
evidence: Verg. A. 2.739: errāvitne viā seu lāpsa resēdit
Ter. Ad. 579: errāvī: in porticum rūrsum redī, of directions given wrongly
terms.comment: Latin says this with the verb: the traveller errat, and the one who gave the directions says errāvī. For “this is the wrong way”, Latin says where the way does not go: Nōn hāc ītur ad forum; of a street with no way through, Terence’s nōn est pervium. Being lost, not knowing where one is, is under “get lost”. Terence’s tōtā errās viā (Eun. 245) is said of a mistaken idea, not of a road.

terms.gloss: stray from the way, go the wrong way
evidence: Cic. Ac. fr. ap. Lact. 6.24: quī in itinere deerrāvissent (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short glosses it “go the wrong way, lose one’s way”; rare, but classical. dē- is short before the vowel.

phrases.latin: Id quidem angiportum nōn est pervium. — Vērum hercle. vah, cēnsēn’ hominem mē esse? errāvī: in porticum rūrsum redī; sānē hāc multō propius ībis et minor est errātiō.
phrases.english: That alley doesn’t go through, though. — True enough. Ugh, and you call me a human being? I got it wrong: go back to the arcade; this way you’ll get there much quicker, and there’s less wandering about.

phrases.latin: substitit, errāvitne viā seu lāpsa resēdit, incertum
phrases.english: whether she stopped, or took the wrong road, or sank down worn out, no one knows

phrases.latin: Errāvimus, mī fīlī: nōn hāc ad forum ītur.
phrases.english: We’ve gone the wrong way, son: this isn’t the way to the square.

sources: Lewis & Short: erro · Lewis & Short: deerro
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 219.
